{{Short description|Study of convergence properties of statistical estimators}}In [[statistics]], '''asymptotic theory''', or '''large sample theory''', is a framework for assessing properties of [[estimator]]s and [[statistical test]]s. Within this framework, it is often assumed that the [[sample size]] {{math|''n''}} may grow indefinitely; the properties of estimators and tests are then evaluated under the limit of {{math|{{nowrap|''n'' → ∞}}}}. In practice, a limit evaluation is considered to be approximately valid for large finite sample sizes too.<ref>Höpfner, R. (2014), Asymptotic Statistics, Walter de Gruyter. 286 pag. {{ISBN|3110250241}}, {{ISBN|978-3110250244}}</ref>

==Overview==
Most statistical problems begin with a dataset of [[sample size|size]] {{math|''n''}}. The asymptotic theory proceeds by assuming that it is possible (in principle) to keep collecting additional data, thus that the sample size grows infinitely, i.e. {{math|''n'' → ∞}}. Under the assumption, many results can be obtained that are unavailable for samples of finite size. An example is the [[law of large numbers|weak law of large numbers]]. The law states that for a sequence of [[independent and identically distributed random variables|independent and identically distributed]] (IID) [[random variable]]s {{math|''X''<sub>1</sub>, ''X''<sub>2</sub>, ...}}, if one value is drawn from each random variable and the average of the first {{math|''n''}} values is computed as {{math|{{overline|''X''}}<sub>''n''</sub>}}, then the {{math|{{overline|''X''}}<sub>''n''</sub>}} [[Convergence of random variables#Convergence in probability|converge in probability]] to the population mean {{math|E[''X<sub>i</sub>'']}} as {{math|{{nowrap|''n'' → ∞}}}}.<ref name=ONE>A. DasGupta (2008), ''Asymptotic Theory of Statistics and Probability'', Springer. {{ISBN|0387759700}}, {{ISBN|978-0387759708}}</ref>

In asymptotic theory, the standard approach is {{math|''n'' → ∞}}. For some [[statistical model]]s, slightly different approaches of asymptotics may be used. For example, with [[panel data]], it is commonly assumed that one dimension in the data remains fixed, whereas the other dimension grows: {{math|{{nowrap|''T'' {{=}} constant}}}} and {{math|''N'' → ∞}}, or vice versa.<ref name=ONE/>

Besides the standard approach to asymptotics, other alternative approaches exist:
* Within the [[local asymptotic normality]] framework, it is assumed that the value of the "true parameter" in the model varies slightly with {{math|''n''}}, such that the {{math|''n''}}-th model corresponds to {{math| ''θ<sub>n</sub>'' {{=}} ''θ'' + ''h''/{{sqrt|''n''}} }}. This approach lets us study the [[regular estimator|regularity of estimators]].
* When [[statistical test]]s are studied for their power to distinguish against the alternatives that are close to the null hypothesis, it is done within the so-called "local alternatives" framework: the null hypothesis is {{math|''H''<sub>0</sub>: ''θ'' {{=}} ''θ''<sub>0</sub>}} and the alternative is {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>: ''θ'' {{=}} ''θ''<sub>0</sub> + ''h''/{{sqrt|''n''}} }}. This approach is especially popular for the [[unit root test]]s.
* There are models where the dimension of the parameter space {{math|Θ<sub>''n''</sub>}} slowly expands with {{math|''n''}}, reflecting the fact that the more observations there are, the more structural effects can be feasibly incorporated in the model.
* In [[kernel density estimation]] and [[kernel regression]], an additional parameter is assumed—the bandwidth {{math|''h''}}. In those models, it is typically taken that {{math|{{nowrap|''h'' → 0}}}} as {{math|{{nowrap|''n'' → ∞}}}}. The rate of convergence must be chosen carefully, though, usually {{math|''h'' ∝ ''n''<sup>−1/5</sup>}}.

In many cases, highly accurate results for finite samples can be obtained via numerical methods (i.e. computers); even in such cases, though, asymptotic analysis can be useful. This point was made by {{Harvtxt|Small|2010|loc=§1.4}}, as follows.
{{quote|text=A primary goal of asymptotic analysis is to obtain a deeper ''qualitative'' understanding of ''quantitative'' tools. The conclusions of an asymptotic analysis often supplement the conclusions which can be obtained by numerical methods.}}

==Modes of convergence of random variables==
{{further|Convergence of random variables}}

==Asymptotic properties==

===Point estimators===
In the following, <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> will be an arbitrary sequence of estimators.

====[[Consistent estimator|Consistency]]====
The sequence <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is said to be ''(weakly)'' ''consistent'', if it [[converges in probability]] to the true value of the parameter being estimated:

<math display="block">\hat\theta_n\ \xrightarrow{\overset{}p}\ \theta_0.</math>

This means that the probability that the estimated value gets arbitrarily close to <math>\theta_0</math> converges to zero as <math>n</math> tends to infinity.<ref name="ONE" /> More specifically, if the convergence of <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> to <math>\theta_0</math> is of [[Big O in probability notation|stochastic order]] <math>1/a_n</math> (also written <math>\textit O_p(1/a_n)</math>) for some sequence <math>(a_n)_{n\in\N}</math> of real numbers diverging to infinity, that is,

<math display="block">\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P(|a_n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)|>K)=0 \quad \text{for all }K>0,</math>

then <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is called ''<math>a_n</math>-consistent''.<ref>Shao (2003), p. 133</ref>

The sequence of estimates is said be ''strongly consistent'', if it even [[Convergence of random variables#Almost sure convergence|converges almost surely]] to the true parameter:

<math display="block">\hat\theta_n\overset{\mathrm{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow}\ \theta_0.</math>

The subtle difference to a weakly consistent estimator is that a strongly consistent estimator is guaranteed to get arbitrarily close to <math>\theta_0</math> as <math>n</math> tends to infinity, eventually.
==== [[Asymptotic distribution]] ====
If it is possible to find sequences of non-random constants <math>(a_n)_{n\in\N}</math>, <math>(b_n)_{n\in\N}</math> (possibly depending on the value <math>\theta_0</math>), and a non-degenerate distribution <math>\mu</math> such that

<math display="block">b_n(\hat\theta_n - a_n)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \mu,</math>

then the sequence of estimators <math>\hat\theta_n</math> is said to have the ''asymptotic distribution'' <math>\mu</math>.

Most often, the asymptotic distribution of estimators encountered in practice is the [[normal distribution]] <math>\mu=\mathcal N(0,V)</math> for some covariance matrix <math>V</math>, in which case the estimator is called ''asymptotically normal''.<ref>Shao (2003), p.70</ref> Some authors require specifically <math>a_n=\theta_0</math> and <math>b_n=\sqrt{n}</math> and then call the sequence of estimators ''asymptotically normal for'' <math>\theta_0</math>.<ref>Lehmann & Casella (1998), p.439</ref>

==== Unbiasedness in the limit ====
The sequence is called ''unbiased in the limit'', if <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]=\theta_0</math>.<ref>Lehmann & Casella (1998), p.431</ref> An estimator with this property is also sometimes called ''approximately unbiased''.<ref>Shao (2003), p.135</ref>

==== Asymptotic unbiasedness ====
The sequence is called ''asymptotically unbiased'' for the parameter <math>\theta_0</math>, if <math>\sigma_n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)</math> [[Convergence of random variables#Convergence in distribution|converges in distribution]] to a random variable <math>G\neq 0</math> with <math>\mathbb{E}[G]=0</math> for some sequence <math>(\sigma_n)_{n\in\N}</math> of real numbers.<ref>Lehmann & Casella (1998), p.438</ref>

==== Limiting variance ====
If there exists a sequence <math>(\tau_n)_{n\in\N}</math> of real numbers such that <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\tau_n\mathrm{Var}({\hat\theta_n})=\sigma^2</math>, then <math>\sigma^2</math> is called the ''limiting variance'' of <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math>. Typically, it is chosen <math>\tau_n=n</math>.<ref>Casella & Berger (2002), p.470</ref>

==== Asymptotic variance ====
If there exists a sequence <math>(b_n)_{n\in\N}</math> such that

<math display="block">b_n(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} G</math>

with <math>0<\mathbb{E}[G^2]<\infty</math>, then <math>V=\mathrm{Var}(G)</math> is called the ''asymptotic variance'' of <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math>.<ref name=":1">Shao (2003), p.138</ref> In particular, if <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is asymptotically unbiased, then <math>V=\mathbb{E}[G^2]</math>.

==== [[Efficiency (statistics)#Asymptotic efficiency|Asymptotic efficiency]] ====
The sequence is called ''asymptotically efficient'', if it is asymptotically normal for <math>\theta_0</math> and its asymptotic variance is <math>V=I(\theta_0)^{-1}</math> with the [[Fisher information]] <math>I(\theta_0)</math>, that is, the asymptotic variance achieves the [[Cramér–Rao bound]].<ref name=":0">Casella & Berger (2002), p.471</ref><ref>Shao (2003), p. 289</ref>

=== Statistical tests ===

====Asymptotic [[confidence region]]s====

== General relations between asymptotic properties ==
As above, let <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> be an arbitrary sequence of estimators.
* If <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is asymptotically normal for <math>\theta_0</math>, then it is consistent (by [[Slutsky's theorem]]).
* If <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is consistent, then it is asymptotically unbiased.<ref>Shao (2003), p.136</ref>
* If <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is asymptotically unbiased and [[Uniform integrability|uniformly integrable]], then it is unbiased in the limit.<ref>Billingsley (1995), p.338</ref> This is the case, for example, when the second moments are uniformly bounded, i.e., <math>\sup_{n\in\N}\mathbb E[|\hat\theta_n|^2]<\infty</math>.
* In the univariate case, if an estimator is asymptotically unbiased and has asymptotic variance <math>\tau^2</math>, and if the limiting variance <math>\sigma^2</math> exists, then <math>\tau^2\leq\sigma^2</math>.<ref name=":0" /> Equility holds if and only if the normalized sequence of estimators, that is <math>b_n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)</math> for suitable <math>b_n</math>, is uniformly integrable (which is often the case in practice).<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

==Asymptotic theorems==
Asymptotic properties of a sequence of estimators <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> (for a parameter <math>\theta</math>) often result from general theorems from [[probability theory]]. In the following, let <math>X_1,X_2,\dots</math> be [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|independent and identically distributed]] observations from the true distribution <math>\mathbb{P}_\theta</math>.

=== For consistency ===

==== Strong law of large numbers ====
If the estimators are of the form <math>\hat\theta_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)</math> for some measurable function <math>f</math> such that <math>\mathbb{E}[|f(X_1)|]<\infty</math>, then by the strong [[law of large numbers]]

<math display="block">\hat\theta_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} \mathbb{E}[f(X_1)].</math>

Thus, if <math>\theta=\mathbb{E}[f(X_1)]</math>, then <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is strongly consistent.

==== Continuous mapping theorem ====
Suppose <math>\theta=f(\tau)</math> for some other parameter <math>\tau</math> and a continuous function <math>f</math>. Given a (strongly) consistent sequence of estimators <math>(\hat\tau_n)_{n\in\N}</math> for the parameter <math>\tau</math>, then by the [[continuous mapping theorem]], the sequence of estimators <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}=(f(\hat\tau_n))_{n\in\N}</math> is (strongly) consistent for the parameter <math>\theta</math>.<ref>Shao (2003), p. 133</ref>

=== For asymptotic distribution ===

==== Central limit theorem ====
If the estimators are of the form <math>\hat\theta_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)</math> for some real-valued measurable function <math>f</math> such that <math>\mathbb{E}[|f(X_1)|^2]<\infty</math>, then by the [[central limit theorem]], <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is asymptotically normal in the sense

<math display="block">\sqrt n\frac{\hat\theta_n-\mu}{\sigma}\ \overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\ \mathcal N(0,1)</math>

with the definitions <math>\mathbb E[f(X_1)]=\mu</math> and <math>\mathrm{Var}(f(X_1))=\sigma^2</math>.

==== Fisher–Tippet–Gnedenko theorem ====
If the estimators are of the form <math>\hat\theta_n=\max_{i=1,\dots,n}f(X_i)</math> for some real-valued measurable function <math>f</math> and if there exists sequences <math>(a_n)_{n\in\N}</math> and <math>(b_n)_{n\in\N}</math> and a non-[[degenerate distribution]] <math>G</math> such that

<math display="block">\frac{\hat\theta_n-a_n}{b_n}\ \overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\ G,</math>

then, by the [[Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem|Fisher–Tippet–Gnedenko theorem]], the asymptotic distribution <math>G</math> of <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is a [[generalized extreme value distribution]].

==== Delta method ====
Suppose <math>\theta=f(\tau)</math> for some other parameter <math>\tau</math> and a differentiable function <math>f</math> with <math>\nabla f(\tau)\neq 0</math>. Given a sequence of estimators <math>(\hat\tau_n)_{n\in\N}</math> for the parameter <math>\tau</math> having asymptotic distribution <math>G</math> in the sense

<math display="block">\frac{\hat\tau_n-\tau}{\sigma_n}\ \overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\ Z\sim G</math>

for some sequence of real numbers <math>(\sigma_n)_{n\in\N}</math>, then by the [[delta method]], the sequence of estimators <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}=(f(\hat\tau_n))_{n\in\N}</math> has asymptotically the distribution of <math>\nabla f(\tau)^\top Z</math>.

In the special case, where <math>(\hat\tau_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is asymptotically normal for <math>\tau</math> with asymptotic variance <math>V</math>, the sequence <math>(\hat\theta_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is asymptotically normal with asymptotic variance <math>\nabla f(\tau)^\top V\nabla f(\tau)</math>.
